title: Salesforce System Architect Primer: Course Completion Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Heavy logging on a frequently accessed Apex class can cause which problem in production?
options: It permanently deletes older captured logs
It disables the org's daily API allocation
The logging itself can make the requests fail
It prevents new trace flags from being created
questions.explanation: A trace flag on a hot class or busy user adds overhead, so production debugging is done surgically with a short-lived flag on the specific path.

questions.question: Four of five sources respond and one times out on a read-side aggregation view. What should the service return?
options: Nothing until every callout completes, so the user never sees a partial view
A response that silently omits the missing block with no indication
The data plus a status naming the missing source, so the page reads as partial
A full retry of the whole fan-out inside the same transaction until all respond
questions.explanation: A read-side aggregation view should return partial results and flag them: the composed data goes back with a status that marks the response incomplete and names the missing source, so the page tells the truth instead of silently omitting a block.

questions.question: What does the principle of least agency add to least privilege for an AI agent?
options: It limits the autonomy itself to the minimum that the task needs, not just the identity's access.
It grants the agent broad autonomy so that it can handle unexpected requests without any human.
It removes the agent user entirely and runs every action as the requesting human instead.
It restricts only the agent's object and field access while leaving its degree of autonomy unconstrained.
questions.explanation: Least agency carries least privilege into autonomy, granting the minimum tool access and credential scope so extra freedom cannot become extra risk.

questions.question: An org offers a public knowledge base that anonymous visitors read and a portal where customers log in to track their own cases. How should external licensing be sized?
options: Every anonymous reader consumes an external license, while logged-in customers consume none.
Both of the audiences share a single site license billed by the number of page views served.
Anonymous readers consume no external license, while each logged-in customer consumes one.
Each logged-in customer is instead given an internal license to keep the portal cost down.
questions.explanation: External licenses attach to users, so a session with no licensed user behind it costs nothing, and a login is what requires the license.

questions.question: What does the pinnacle architect credential require beyond the domain certifications?
options: Three separate multiple-choice exams covering every certification domain
Documented real work and a scenario defense before a review board
A recertification pass every six months.
A written recommendation from three prior employers.
questions.explanation: The pinnacle credential requires both domain credentials plus documented real work and a live review-board defense, so it cannot be earned by study alone.

questions.question: An interactive turn must stay fast while a bulk path handles high volume. How should throughput and latency be treated?
options: Maximize throughput first, then check whether latency still meets the target.
Treat them as one axis, since improving either one always improves the other.
Pick a latency target, then push throughput up without breaking it.
Set them independently, because they never trade off against each other.
questions.explanation: Latency and throughput are separate axes that trade against each other, so the right move is to fix a latency target and then raise throughput as high as it can go within that target.

questions.question: Multiple records describe the same real-world customer. What does linking them into one profile actually do?
options: It selects a winning value and overwrites the source records.
It creates a golden record that replaces all the originals.
It links records for a use without overwriting sources.
It guarantees every linked field is complete and accurate.
questions.explanation: Identity resolution links records so the right source value can be chosen for a given use; it is not a golden record and does not overwrite source data. Treating unify-as-overwrite destroys the traceability that governance and lineage depend on.

questions.question: Accessibility guidance is organized around a small set of high-level principles rather than a flat symptom list. Which option is one of those principles?
options: Aesthetic
Adaptive
Scalable
Robust
questions.explanation: The four principles are perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Every specific success criterion is an expression of one of them.

questions.question: A user who can see an Opportunity can also see its parent Account, though no rule or share record was created. What explains this?
options: A sharing rule opened the Account to that user.
The account hierarchy rolled access up from the opportunity.
Parent implicit sharing for standard parent-child pairs.
A manual share created automatically by the opportunity owner.
questions.explanation: Implicit sharing is native and cannot be turned off: seeing a child opportunity, case, contact, or order grants access to the associated account, without any rule or share record.

questions.question: A design enqueues one asynchronous job per record while iterating a large query. Why is this a problem?
options: Async capacity is a shared org-level budget, so cost scales with record count.
Each job runs in its own transaction, which is the safest option for isolation.
Async limits are allocated per feature, so one job per record cannot affect others.
Queueable jobs cannot accept sObjects, so the design will not compile at all.
questions.explanation: Asynchronous capacity is an org-level budget shared with every other feature, so a job per record multiplies the shared cost by the record count and hits the per-transaction enqueue cap.

questions.question: A five-year cost model lists only licences, implementation, operations, maintenance, integration and change. A reviewer says the case is too optimistic. What is the likely gap?
options: It omits indirect costs such as organizational load and technical debt interest.
It counts maintenance as a direct line, which is really a one-time implementation cost.
It includes change, which does not belong in a cost model at all.
It is complete, because those six lines are the full set of costs.
questions.explanation: Those are the six direct lines, but total cost of ownership also carries indirect costs: organizational load, technical debt interest, governance overhead and unused functionality. For mature solutions the indirect costs often exceed the direct ones.

questions.question: A client wants near-zero data loss on financial records but currently only takes daily backups. What is required beyond the daily backup?
options: Nothing more at all, because a daily backup already achieves near-zero data loss for financial records on its own without any extra tooling.
A replication mechanism such as asynchronous event streaming or change data capture, because daily backups cap data loss at a day.
A longer backup retention period, because keeping many older copies on hand reduces the amount of data lost in an outage.
A written service level agreement with the vendor that contractually waives any data loss during an outage.
questions.explanation: A daily backup can never produce a sub-day recovery point, so a near-zero objective on financial records demands a replication mechanism such as event streaming or change data capture, not simply more frequent copies.

questions.question: Which condition makes Bulk API 2.0 the right choice over a synchronous API?
options: A single record that must be confirmed before the user continues.
A call that needs a strongly typed, compile-time WSDL contract to catch errors.
A large volume where the caller does not need to wait for the result.
A small batch that must all succeed or fail as one operation.
questions.explanation: Bulk is asynchronous and built for scale, so it fits large volumes where no one is waiting, while small or all-or-nothing calls stay synchronous.

questions.question: A dashboard figure is disputed. What makes lineage the authoritative answer?
options: It reruns the report until the very same number is reproduced again.
It records the data's origin and every transformation applied.
It stores a snapshot of the raw layer for each report.
It names the engineer who originally built the dashboard.
questions.explanation: Lineage is the traceable record of where data originated and every transformation it passed through. It must span from the source system to the consuming report, because any untraceable hop breaks the chain and turns the answer into a guess.

questions.question: Why does a middleware hub beat point-to-point wiring as systems multiply?
options: Pairwise connections grow with the square of the system count; a hub grows linearly.
Point-to-point wiring is always faster to build and far cheaper to maintain over time.
A hub removes the need for any authentication between connected systems.
Point-to-point connections stop working once three systems exist.
questions.explanation: Every pair of systems needs its own connection, so point-to-point count grows with the square of systems while a hub needs each system to connect only once.

questions.question: A company wants customers and partners to log into a portal. Which approach fits, and which one is the anti-pattern?
options: A community with internal Salesforce licenses, to save cost
A connected app with the username-password flow
A single sign-on setting that points partners at employee roles
A community with external licenses, never internal ones
questions.explanation: External customers and partners belong on Experience Cloud sites with external licenses; using internal licenses for outside users is explicitly discouraged.

questions.question: A consumer keeps double-counting the same events after it restarts. What causes this, and what is the fix?
options: Exactly-once delivery failed somewhere in the broker, and the fix is to switch the cluster to a stronger consistency and isolation setting across every partition.
At-least-once delivery re-reads events after a restart, and the fix is to make the consumer idempotent or deduplicate on a stable event ID.
The retention window expired, and the fix is to store a private copy of every event the consumer reads.
The consumer group is unbalanced, and the fix is to add more consumers to rebalance the partitions.
questions.explanation: Streaming platforms default to at-least-once, so a consumer that crashes before committing its offset re-reads events on restart; the design must tolerate that duplicate by making the sink idempotent or deduplicating on an event ID.

questions.question: Pre-launch testing is not sufficient as a governance control for an AI system. Why?
options: Model behavior stays fixed after ship, so a single sign-off is enough
Its behavior drifts as data or the vendor's version changes over time
Reviewing lower-risk systems is prohibited by regulation
Model outputs stay correct in production however they were tested
questions.explanation: A model is not stable after ship: its output distribution shifts as the data or the vendor's version changes, so governance needs ongoing monitoring as part of the structure, not only a pre-launch check.

questions.question: Why is a branching strategy best treated as a governance decision rather than a tooling detail?
options: The branching strategy is a governance decision that sets who may merge, how often, and what must be true first.
The branching strategy is a tooling detail that only affects where files are physically stored and how quickly they can be checked out.
The branching strategy matters only for teams that have never adopted continuous integration or automated testing.
The branching strategy can safely be deferred until the team is already under pressure to ship a release.
questions.explanation: The branching strategy decides who can merge, how often, and what has to be true before a merge is allowed; without that decision, teams accumulate merge conflicts that surface at the worst possible moment, release time.

questions.question: A candidate plans to present three viable architectures and let the judges choose among them. What is wrong with that approach?
options: Nothing, because letting the board choose among options demonstrates openness and collaboration.
Only a problem if the judges specifically ask the candidate for a recommendation.
A clear recommendation is missing, because leading with options reads as unresolved advice.
Nothing, provided each option is described in the same amount of detail by the candidate.
questions.explanation: Providing options without a recommendation reads as sloppy advisory. The presentation should lead with a recommendation and treat the other choices as rejected alternatives with reasons.

questions.question: Two users sit at the same level of the role hierarchy. Does one automatically see the other's records?
options: Yes, because peers in a role always share each other's records
Yes, if they both report to the same manager
No, access flows up the hierarchy but not between peers
No, unless the object is set to Public Read Write
questions.explanation: The role hierarchy grants a manager the access of the people below, but peers in the same role do not inherit each other's records.

questions.question: When does batching hurt more than it helps?
options: When an interactive user's result would be delayed to fill a larger batch.
When many independent requests can share the same expensive compute step.
When a nightly job enriches a large batch that nobody is actively waiting on.
When requests arrive together and can each tolerate a small wait.
questions.explanation: Batching is a throughput tool with a latency cost, so it is wrong when one waiting user is made to pay that cost to enlarge the batch.

questions.question: What does running a restore drill actually establish that an untested backup cannot?
options: That the backup can be restored within the target recovery time and loses no more than the allowed data, proven by a timed test.
That the backup files exist, are complete, and are stored in a separate location from the source data, safely out of reach of the primary org.
That the platform's infrastructure-level failover between data centers is functioning exactly as the vendor designed it.
That the recovery runbook has been written, reviewed, and formally approved by the business stakeholders before any incident.
questions.explanation: A backup is only as real as the restore you have performed; a drill times the actual recovery against the RTO and measures the data lost against the RPO, exposing the gap between the plan and reality while the stakes are a sandbox.

questions.question: Which contrast correctly separates an agent from a workflow?
options: A workflow uses several models, while an agent uses only one.
A workflow follows fixed code paths, while an agent lets the model choose steps at runtime.
A workflow cannot call tools at all, while an agent always calls at least one tool during its run.
A workflow runs on a server, while an agent runs on the end user's device.
questions.explanation: In a workflow the control flow lives in code, while an agent lets the model decide at runtime which tool to call and whether to continue, so the control flow lives partly in the model.

questions.question: What does a master-detail relationship provide that a lookup relationship does not?
options: Inherited detail security and roll-up summaries on the master.
An independent security model and a visible Owner field on the detail.
A way to relate two objects that otherwise have no relationship.
The ability to store one record inside two different objects.
questions.explanation: Master-detail makes the master own the detail, so the detail inherits the master's security and ownership and roll-ups become available; a lookup supports neither.

questions.question: What does enabling the Salesforce CDN for the Lightning component framework actually deliver?
options: It caches the org's record data and metadata so that records are served from a location nearer the user.
It caches the framework's static script and JSON files for faster loads, not record data or metadata.
It replaces the client-side data cache completely, so that Lightning Data Service is no longer needed.
It is already enabled inside every org, so the setting needs no review during a performance pass.
questions.explanation: The CDN accelerates delivery of the framework files themselves; it never carries your org's records or metadata.

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, which controls does the customer design?
options: The physical data center, the network perimeter, and the platform.
Who may log in, what they may do, and how systems authenticate.
The provider's encryption services and its compliance certificates.
Nothing beyond choosing which cloud platform the company buys.
questions.explanation: The provider secures the cloud; the customer secures the org. That means defining who can log in, what they can do, how data is classified, and how integrations authenticate, rather than inheriting responsibility for controls never designed.

questions.question: Which split correctly describes the two architect domains?
options: System: integration and identity; Application: data and sharing
System: data and sharing; Application: integration and identity
System: end-user training; Application: release governance
System: native features; Application: security reviews
questions.explanation: The Application Architect owns everything inside the org, such as the data model and sharing, while the System Architect owns what crosses between systems: integration, identity, and release governance.

questions.question: A design states that the solution must be fast and reliable and that every feature needs near-total uptime. What is the core problem with those targets?
options: They are unmeasurable, so they drive no architecture decisions.
They are pitched too low for any customer-facing application to accept.
They should match the platform commitment exactly.
They belong in the deck rather than the spreadsheet.
questions.explanation: A target with no number, no percentile and no stated measurement cannot drive a design choice or be proven before go-live. A uniform maximum also ignores that business criticality differs between revenue operations and internal tools.

questions.question: What single principle distinguishes federation from replication when the org needs external data?
options: The data is copied into the org and kept aligned by a pipeline
The data stays at the source and the query is pushed to it
The data is cached in the browser after one full download
The data is loaded nightly into a big object for local querying
questions.explanation: Federation leaves the data in place and moves the computation to it: Salesforce sends the query to the source and renders only the matching rows, whereas replication copies the data in and owns keeping the two copies aligned.

questions.question: Which situation is a legitimate structural reason to run a second Salesforce org?
options: A line of business that wants its own space because the shared org's request backlog is slow.
A regulatory requirement that needs structural isolation and reviewability a sharing model cannot provide.
An org that has simply grown large and slow, so that adding a second instance will make it noticeably faster again.
A team that wants a single unified 360-degree view of every customer across the whole company.
questions.explanation: A split is warranted only when the wall itself is the requirement; local control and speed belong inside one org with better governance.

questions.question: A bulk integration writes to a lookup target that hundreds of thousands of records already point at, and saves start throwing lock exceptions. What is the fix?
options: Add many more child records to spread the lock out more widely
Distribute the values across more targets or use a picklist
Remove the owner from the record so it stops locking
Increase the lookup field length to reduce contention
questions.explanation: Lookup skew is eased by reducing lock frequency and duration, such as spreading the associated records across more values or replacing the object with a picklist.

questions.question: A candidate completes Platform Developer, Platform Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, Platform Identity and Access Management Architect and Platform Integration Architect. Which credential does that set grant?
options: Application Architect
Technical Architect
Platform Data Architect
System Architect
questions.explanation: System Architect is granted by that set of four exams, which lean toward the systems around one org and the life of the solution after go-live. Application Architect is a different set, and Technical Architect sits above both.

questions.question: Two systems both claim to own the same piece of data. Why is this the failure that unravels a scenario solution?
options: Because it doubles the storage cost of that data across every system in the client environment, slows every query that reads it, and forces constant reconciliation.
Because when a fact has two owners the copies drift, and any view built on that fact becomes unreliable, so each fact needs one owner.
Because the second owner always performs more slowly than the first one under any realistic production load.
Because it prevents the use of the platform's standard objects for that particular entity in the data model.
questions.explanation: One fact must have one owner; when two systems both claim it, the copies drift apart and take any joined customer view down with them, which is why fixing the system of record comes before integration and data modeling.

questions.question: What value does continuous integration add to a Salesforce team's delivery lifecycle?
options: It replaces the need for a branching strategy entirely by merging all work directly into production on a fixed schedule every night.
It merges every change into a shared main line often and validates each merge, so integration problems surface early and cheaply.
It removes the need for source control because every change is automatically tested before it can reach the production org.
It ships every change straight to production on each merge without any separate validation or review step.
questions.explanation: Continuous integration validates every merge to the shared main line, so a change that breaks the build is caught the day it is merged rather than the week before release, when the fix is far more expensive.

questions.question: A fan-out must call several external systems on every page load, and one is slow. What is the sound first response for a read-side aggregation view?
options: Fire all the calls synchronously and accept that the slow system delays the page
Cache the composed result or move the fan-out off the request path
Raise the per-transaction callout limit above one hundred
Let the browser issue the callouts to each external system directly
questions.explanation: The cumulative time for external callouts in one transaction is bounded, and a slow system consumes budget the others need, so a frequently viewed read-side view should cache the composed answer or push the fan-out off the synchronous path rather than pay the full cost per visit.

questions.question: What makes a golden set trustworthy as the anchor for regression runs?
options: It holds only hand-written happy-path examples that the system already passes.
It is built once and frozen so the baseline never moves again.
It mirrors production traffic, including edge and adversarial cases.
It scores model outputs with fluency measures such as perplexity and BLEU.
questions.explanation: A set that does not reproduce real traffic is a biased design, and because production keeps changing the set has to be grown and refreshed to stay a faithful reference.

questions.question: A recorded decision has changed. What does good practice say to do?
options: Edit the original accepted record to reflect the new decision
Delete the old record so the log always stays current
Keep both records with no indication of which one is still active
Write a new record that supersedes the old one and links the two
questions.explanation: An accepted record is never edited; a superseding record preserves the history of the thinking and shows when and why the direction shifted.

questions.question: Once a change set has been uploaded, what recovery does it give you if the deployment breaks production?
options: A one-click rollback to the previous deployed version
An automatic snapshot of the whole target org taken at deploy time
None built in; the prior state must be reconstructed by hand
A reverse package that the platform generates automatically
questions.explanation: Change sets keep no pre-deployment snapshot and offer no undo, so reversing a bad deployment depends on records kept outside the tool.

questions.question: A single transaction calls update once on a list of 12,000 records. Why does it fail?
options: The 150-statement DML limit is exceeded by the bulk call
The 10,000-row DML limit is exceeded even though one statement was issued
The 50,000-row SOQL retrieval limit is exceeded by the query
The cumulative callout timeout is exceeded by the callouts that were made
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are separate governors: one update call is a single statement but processes 12,000 rows, past the 10,000-row ceiling.

questions.question: A candidate plans to present every option considered and let the judges pick the one they prefer. What does published guidance to candidates say?
options: Present one recommended solution, with the choice justified.
Present several options whenever more than one design is viable.
Let the judges choose so the panel feels involved in the decision.
Present options only when each one is fully costed for the panel.
questions.explanation: The published guidance is to present recommended solutions and not options, and to justify why the solution should be used. A menu reads as an unresolved design, and the board scores a decision with its trade-off attached.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a memory layer to the question it answers?
options: Semantic memory answers what happened; episodic memory answers what is true.
Procedural memory stores domain facts; semantic memory stores routines.
Working memory stores durable facts; long-term memory holds the window.
Semantic memory is what is true; episodic memory is what happened.
questions.explanation: Semantic memory holds durable facts about what is true, while episodic memory records time-indexed experiences and answers what happened.

questions.question: A Message Router receives one message and must deliver it to one of several channels. What discipline keeps it a router rather than a router and translator combined?
options: It decides the destination only and forwards the payload unchanged.
It rewrites the payload into the target format before forwarding it.
It merges several related messages into one combined payload first.
It holds the message until every downstream channel confirms receipt.
questions.explanation: A router answers only where a message goes; reshaping the payload belongs to a separate translator, which keeps routing rules simple and testable.

questions.question: A batch finishes comfortably in a full copy sandbox but takes much longer in production. What does the sandbox result actually establish?
options: It establishes data-volume behavior only, not concurrency or overlapping job schedules.
It establishes production capacity, because a full copy holds production-like data volumes.
It establishes concurrency behavior, because the sandbox serves the same user mix.
It establishes peak behavior, because the sandbox reproduces the month-end load.
questions.explanation: A sandbox proves data-volume behavior; it does not reproduce the real user mix, the overlapping job schedule, or shared-infrastructure effects, so its timing is a floor rather than a prediction.

questions.question: A scenario gives 40 million records, a ten-year retention rule and a three-second dashboard. What does a strong data answer do?
options: Store everything in a single object and rely on list view filters over it.
Increase the record limit by moving the org to a larger edition.
Answer with the record count alone, since volume is the constraint.
Split by operation, using a summarized layer and an archive at scale.
questions.explanation: Volume questions are really questions about which operations run over the records. A strong answer separates the requirements by operation: a summarized layer for the dashboard, an operational window with indexed filters, and an archive for the retained history.

questions.question: An object has four separate triggers, each querying the same related records. What is the problem and the recommended fix?
options: Each trigger keeps its own governor budget, so separating them improves isolation.
All logic should move into the trigger file so that nothing is shared across files.
They share one budget and fire unordered; use one trigger per object that routes to a handler.
Multiple triggers are safe whenever each one stays short, readable, and clearly named for its purpose.
questions.explanation: Multiple triggers on one object draw from the same budget and have no guaranteed firing order; a single thin trigger per object that delegates restores ordered execution and predictable budget use.

questions.question: Two users open the same Lightning page in the same org and see different experienced page time. What best explains this?
options: Experienced page time is measured entirely on the server, so it cannot vary between any two users.
The org configuration differs for each user, which is the only factor that shapes the load time.
Network conditions and device capability set a floor outside the org's control, so the same page differs.
The difference proves a defect, because the platform is supposed to serve every single user an identical page load.
questions.explanation: Only org configuration is yours to engineer; the network, device, and browser of each user set a floor you cannot control.

questions.question: What turns a non-functional requirement from a vague wish into a testable target?
options: A statement that the system should be fast and reliable
A measurable value paired with a condition, such as a time bound
A list of the technologies the delivery team prefers
A reference to the vendor framework that names the quality attribute
questions.explanation: A quality requirement is a target you can test, so it pairs a number with a condition rather than a general aspiration.

questions.question: A change set can move metadata between which orgs?
options: Any two orgs that share a namespace prefix
Org pairs affiliated with the same production org
Any two orgs connected by a deployment user
Orgs in different companies running the same edition
questions.explanation: A change set travels only between related orgs, meaning orgs sharing a production org, and it carries metadata rather than data records.

questions.question: What question does IP allowlisting answer, and how does it relate to strong authentication?
options: It proves the caller's identity cryptographically and can replace token validation entirely.
It encrypts all traffic in transit, so separate authentication tokens become unnecessary.
It restricts which network ranges may reach the app, a layer on top of strong auth.
It verifies the caller's certificate chain each time during the connection handshake.
questions.explanation: Allowlisting answers a cruder, earlier question, whether the caller is even from a recognized place, so it is defense in depth and not a replacement for proving identity.

questions.question: An org needs to read another org's master data in real time with no middleware in the path. Which mechanism fits?
options: Salesforce-to-Salesforce shared records, which link the two orgs natively and remain suited to new designs.
Platform events published from one org, which cross the org boundary on their own without a relay.
A nightly batch job that copies the master data into a local object held inside the other org.
Salesforce Connect with the cross-org adapter, which reads the other org through the standard REST API.
questions.explanation: The cross-org adapter uses the platform's own REST API directly between the orgs, with the source org's authentication and permissions.

questions.question: Why does reaching for a named credential reduce the risk that a secret leaks into source control?
options: It encrypts every callout payload so the secret stays unreadable in transit.
It keeps the endpoint and authentication in setup, so code never holds the secret.
It rotates the stored secret automatically on a fixed nightly schedule.
It blocks every call that does not originate from a trusted address inside the org.
questions.explanation: When the endpoint and the credential live in setup and the code calls the credential by name, there is no secret string for anyone to paste into code and commit.

questions.question: Every new integration keeps reinterpreting the shared customer record differently across systems. Which standing decision contains that problem?
options: Force every system to rename its local fields to match the CRM.
Agree one canonical shape that every system maps to and from.
Move all enterprise data into one store so no mapping is needed.
Let each integration define its own mapping and document it apart.
questions.explanation: A canonical data model names one agreed representation for the objects that cross systems, and each system maps to and from it at its own boundary. This does not remove the differences; it contains them in one place so new integrations do not reinvent the mapping.

questions.question: When is a synchronous call the right choice for a step in a pipeline?
options: When the caller needs the result before it can continue
When the caller wants to keep working while the work runs
When the downstream system is slow or frequently down
When the work is high volume and low priority
questions.explanation: A synchronous call blocks the caller for the full round trip, which is the right trade when the caller cannot proceed without the result.

questions.question: A team transfers a set of components to another org as an unmanaged package. What does the receiving org end up with?
options: A one-time copy it owns, with no versioning and no upgrade path
A source-protected bundle the originator hides from every receiver
A locked bundle only the originator can later modify or upgrade
A versioned bundle the originator can upgrade on demand
questions.explanation: An unmanaged package is a one-time copy: after install its components belong to the receiving org, editable and deletable, with no link back to the source and no way to push an upgrade. Locked components, source protection, and upgrade paths belong to managed packages.

questions.question: The four allowed design artifacts each own exactly one job. Which pairing is correct?
options: The document is the record of decisions, and the spreadsheet makes numbers defensible.
The document carries the numbers, and the diagram is where the whole narrative is written.
The spreadsheet is the spatial argument, and the deck stores the decision log.
The diagram stores the requirement register, and the deck holds the NFR table.
questions.explanation: The document leads as the record of requirements and decisions, the diagram makes the spatial argument, the sheet quantifies, and the deck persuades. Letting one artifact do another's job costs minutes you do not have.

questions.question: When sizing an integration, which decision should come first?
options: Whether the caller can wait for a response.
Which API the architect prefers to use.
Which format the source system already speaks.
How many licenses the org happens to own.
questions.explanation: Whether the caller can wait separates synchronous from asynchronous options before volume and format matter.

questions.question: A composite call returns HTTP 200 even though a subrequest failed and rolled back. What does a correct handler do?
options: Treat the 200 status as proof the whole call succeeded
Retry the entire call with exponential backoff
Route the call straight to the dead-letter channel
Inspect the response body for failed subrequests
questions.explanation: A composite request can return HTTP 200 while individual subrequests fail and roll back, so correctness depends on reading the response body, not only the status code.

questions.question: When should an integration use the request-reply pattern?
options: When the caller must wait and act on the response immediately.
When the caller hands off the work and never waits for any result.
When large volumes move on a nightly schedule.
When data must be replicated in bulk in either direction.
questions.explanation: Request-reply is synchronous: the caller blocks for the response and updates its state from it, which only works for small, real-time interactions.

questions.question: When is Platform Cache the right lever?
options: For large result sets that must always stay fully up to date
For small stable values read far more often than they change
For per-user values that change on every request
For values that the application code itself mutates on every transaction
questions.explanation: Caching removes the need to run the query at all, so it fits values that are stable and hot rather than large or rapidly changing ones.
